Road Traffic Accidents in Greater Bangkok, 2022

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

Spatial concentration, fatal-event proximity and implications for road safety

An R-based point-pattern study of 3,599 recorded accidents across Bangkok and five surrounding provinces.
Author

Zhenhua Liu

Exercise home · Executive summary · Reproduce this study · GitHub source

NoteStudy in brief

The analysis covers 3,599 geolocated accident records, including 159 fatal accidents, within Bangkok and five neighbouring provinces in 2022. Recorded accidents concentrate along metropolitan corridors. Their spatial pattern differs strongly from uniform placement, but fatal accidents do not show excess close-pair clustering relative to the observed accident locations after accounting for province and reporting agency. These findings support corridor screening and improvements to reporting coverage; they do not estimate the probability of a crash per journey.

1 Research question and scope

Where do recorded accidents concentrate in Greater Bangkok, how does their frequency vary during 2022, and are fatal accidents unusually close to one another after accounting for the geography of reported accidents?

The intended audience is metropolitan transport planners and road-safety teams. Three distinctions guide the study:

  1. Intensity: the number of recorded events per unit area or calendar day.
  2. Second-order structure: how event pairs are distributed over distance, relative to a stated random model.
  3. Risk: the probability of an accident for a given amount of travel. Traffic volumes, vehicle-kilometres and consistent reporting denominators are unavailable, so risk is not estimated.

The unit of analysis is an accident record identified by acc_code, rather than a casualty or vehicle. A fatal accident has number_of_fatalities > 0; one such accident can contain several deaths. All accident types are included. Presumed causes are not treated as established causal explanations.

2 Data preparation

2.1 Sources, coverage and provenance

Input Coverage and version Use and license
Thailand Road Accident 2019–2022, published by thaweewatboy Nationwide, 2019–2022; portal last updated 19 August 2023; accessed 27 September 2026 Incident records; CC0, as stated in the saved Kaggle metadata
geoBoundaries gbOpen THA ADM1 77 administrative areas; metadata vintage 2017; boundary ID THA-ADM1-36821470; accessed 27 September 2026 Study boundary; ODbL 1.0, upstream OpenStreetMap contributors and Wambacher
Thailand NSO: Bangkok and Vicinities Official regional grouping Geographic definition, not an accident denominator

The original CSV contains 18 columns covering identifiers, dates, province, reporting agency, accident attributes, casualties and coordinates. The source has no traffic exposure or coordinate-accuracy measure. Its records come from three road agencies, so it cannot be assumed to enumerate every accident on every local street.

The download manifest, Kaggle metadata and boundary metadata preserve acquisition dates, versions and SHA-256 checksums. The boundary downloader uses a fixed repository revision. Raw files remain separate from analytical outputs.

Code 
raw <- read_csv(file.path(ex_dir,'data/raw/thai_road_accident_2019_2022.csv'),
  col_types=cols(incident_datetime=col_character(), report_datetime=col_character()),
  show_col_types=FALSE)
boundaries <- st_read(file.path(ex_dir,'data/raw/geoBoundaries-THA-ADM1.geojson'),quiet=TRUE)
stopifnot(nrow(problems(raw)) == 0)
raw$incident_date <- as.Date(substr(raw$incident_datetime,1,10))
stopifnot(!anyNA(raw$incident_date))

2.2 Study extent, dates and coordinates

The study area comprises Bangkok, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Samut Prakan, Samut Sakhon and Nakhon Pathom. These are selected by administrative ISO codes TH-10, TH-12, TH-13, TH-11, TH-74 and TH-73. Their dissolved union forms the observation window; it is not the rectangular map extent. Province labels in the CSV serve as a quality check, while polygon intersection determines spatial inclusion.

The analysis uses incident dates from 1 January to 31 December 2022, inclusive. Dates are read as written, without converting an unspecified source timezone. The reporting date is not substituted for the incident date. Monthly counts are divided by each month’s number of calendar days; a single year supports description, not a claim of recurring seasonality.

Longitude and latitude are interpreted as WGS 84 because they are supplied as geographic coordinates. This source-CRS assumption is a limitation. They are transformed to WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647), appropriate for the region’s longitude and metre-based analysis. Province geometries are validated before union. The older boundary vintage is disclosed; this study does not establish that every local boundary was unchanged between 2017 and 2022.

Code 
d2022 <- filter(raw, incident_date >= as.Date('2022-01-01'), incident_date < as.Date('2023-01-01'))
unique_records <- distinct(d2022)
# A duplicated ID with conflicting attributes requires investigation, not an arbitrary drop.
stopifnot(!anyNA(unique_records$acc_code), !anyDuplicated(unique_records$acc_code))
valid <- unique_records |> filter(is.finite(longitude),is.finite(latitude),
  between(longitude,-180,180),between(latitude,-90,90))
plausible <- valid |> filter(between(longitude,97,106),between(latitude,5,21))
audit <- data.frame(stage=c('Original records, all years','Incident year 2022',
  'After removing identical rows','Valid global coordinates','Plausible Thailand coordinates'),
  retained=c(nrow(raw),nrow(d2022),nrow(unique_records),nrow(valid),nrow(plausible)))
Code 
iso6 <- c('TH-10','TH-12','TH-13','TH-11','TH-74','TH-73')
provinces <- boundaries[match(iso6,boundaries$shapeISO),] |>
  st_make_valid() |> st_transform(32647)
provinces$province <- sub(' Province$','',provinces$shapeName)
stopifnot(nrow(provinces)==6, all(st_is_valid(provinces)))
study_window <- st_union(provinces)
points_all <- st_as_sf(plausible,coords=c('longitude','latitude'),crs=4326,remove=FALSE) |> st_transform(32647)
hits <- st_intersects(points_all,provinces)
points <- points_all[lengths(hits)>0,]
# Shared-boundary points use the first province in the declared ISO order.
points$spatial_province <- provinces$province[vapply(hits[lengths(hits)>0],`[`,integer(1),1)]
points$fatal <- points$number_of_fatalities > 0
stopifnot(!anyNA(points$fatal),all(points$number_of_fatalities>=0),
  !anyNA(points$number_of_injuries),all(points$number_of_injuries>=0))
audit <- rbind(audit,data.frame(stage='Within six-province study window',retained=nrow(points)))
audit$removed_from_previous <- c(NA,-diff(audit$retained))
xy <- st_coordinates(points)
loc_key <- paste(points$longitude,points$latitude,sep=',')
points$location_id <- match(loc_key,unique(loc_key))
quality <- list(n_total=nrow(raw),n_2022=nrow(d2022),n=nrow(points),
  area_km2=as.numeric(st_area(study_window))/1e6,
  unique_locations=length(unique(loc_key)),repeated_extra=sum(duplicated(loc_key)),
  repeated_sites=sum(table(loc_key)>1),max_at_site=max(table(loc_key)),
  fatalities=sum(points$number_of_fatalities),fatal_events=sum(points$fatal),
  injuries=sum(points$number_of_injuries),
  province_mismatch=sum(points$province_en!=points$spatial_province),
  labelled_six=sum(d2022$province_en %in% provinces$province),
  labelled_six_invalid=sum(unique_records$province_en %in% provinces$province &
    (!is.finite(unique_records$latitude)|!is.finite(unique_records$longitude))),
  shared_boundary=sum(lengths(hits)>1))
missing_summary <- unique_records |>
  filter(!is.finite(longitude)|!is.finite(latitude)) |>
  count(province_en,agency,sort=TRUE)
label_audit <- data.frame(
  category=c('Label in study area; located inside','Label in study area; located outside',
             'Label outside study area; located inside','Label in study area; missing coordinates'),
  events=c(sum(points$province_en %in% provinces$province),
    sum(plausible$province_en %in% provinces$province)-sum(points$province_en %in% provinces$province),
    sum(!points$province_en %in% provinces$province),quality$labelled_six_invalid))
province_summary <- points |> st_drop_geometry() |> group_by(spatial_province) |>
  summarise(events=n(),fatal_events=sum(fatal),fatalities=sum(number_of_fatalities),
    injuries=sum(number_of_injuries),.groups='drop')
province_summary$area_km2 <- as.numeric(st_area(provinces[match(province_summary$spatial_province,provinces$province),]))/1e6
province_summary$events_per_km2 <- province_summary$events/province_summary$area_km2
agency_summary <- points |> st_drop_geometry() |> count(agency,sort=TRUE)
write_csv(audit,file.path(out_dir,'audit.csv'))
write_csv(province_summary,file.path(out_dir,'province-summary.csv'))
write_csv(agency_summary,file.path(out_dir,'agency-summary.csv'))
write_csv(missing_summary,file.path(out_dir,'missing-coordinate-summary.csv'))
write_csv(label_audit,file.path(out_dir,'label-audit.csv'))

The resulting window covers 7,604 km², measured from these polygons. All 3,599 retained points intersect this window; no point falls on a shared province boundary in this dataset.

2.3 Cleaning audit

No identical rows or duplicate accident IDs were found among the 2022 records. The script stops if conflicting duplicate IDs appear in a future input. Missing or non-finite coordinates are excluded from spatial analysis; valid geographic ranges are checked before projection. A broad Thailand bounding check removes no additional records. Points outside the six-province union are then excluded.

Missingness is geographically and institutionally concentrated. All 189 2022 records without coordinates are labelled Bangkok and reported by the Expressway Authority of Thailand. They account for 9.5% of the 1,990 Bangkok-labelled records. They are not imputed at a province centroid, because this would create an artificial hotspot. Consequently, mapped Bangkok expressway intensity may be understated.

Four geolocated records labelled within the six provinces fall outside the polygon union; ten labelled outside fall inside. Among the retained points, 14 have different text and spatial province labels. Spatial assignment is used consistently, without claiming either source is error-free.

There are 3,278 distinct recorded coordinate pairs. 199 sites contain more than one accident, with 321 additional records beyond one per site and a maximum of 16 records at one location. Different accident IDs at the same coordinates remain separate events: repeat accidents and geocoding to common reference points are both possible. Sensitivity checks address their influence. Coordinates are not randomly jittered to make the pattern appear more precise.

2.4 Study-area map

Code 
labels <- st_point_on_surface(provinces)
overview <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data=provinces,fill='#eef2f5',colour='#718093',linewidth=.4) +
  geom_sf(data=points,aes(colour=fatal),size=.65,alpha=.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c('FALSE'='#217c91','TRUE'='#ce3b3b'),
    labels=c('Non-fatal recorded accident','At least one recorded death'),name=NULL) +
  geom_sf_text(data=labels,aes(label=province),size=3.2,fontface='bold',check_overlap=TRUE) +
  labs(title='Recorded accidents follow metropolitan corridors',
    subtitle=paste(format(nrow(points),big.mark=','),'events within the six-province boundary, 2022'),
    caption='Kaggle: Thai road accidents | geoBoundaries ADM1 (2017) | WGS 84 / UTM 47N; graticule in degrees') +
  theme(legend.position='bottom',axis.title=element_blank())
save_plot('study-area',overview)
print(audit); print(quality); print(province_summary); print(agency_summary)

Interpretation. Bangkok contains 1,802 retained records, about half the study total. Dense alignments extend into Samut Prakan, Pathum Thani and Samut Sakhon, whereas western Nakhon Pathom has fewer observations. Fatal events occur beyond the densest Bangkok alignments. The map therefore suggests that accident frequency and fatal-event geography warrant separate attention. These are recorded locations: overlapping symbols obscure repeated coordinates, and sparse areas may reflect road-agency coverage as well as fewer accidents. The missing Bangkok expressway coordinates further limit direct comparisons.

3 First-order analysis: intensity across space and time

3.1 Methods and parameter choices

Monthly events per day provide a transparent temporal description. Spatial intensity is estimated with a Gaussian planar kernel density estimator (KDE), using each event with weight one. The primary smoothing scale is 2 km, with 1 km and 3 km alternatives. These are declared regional screening scales, not a statistically optimal junction-level bandwidth. A common 250 m grid provides four cells per smallest bandwidth and eight per primary bandwidth.

The spatstat.explore::density.ppp() edge correction compensates for kernel mass outside the observation window. Densities calculated per square metre are multiplied by one million to give recorded events per km² for 2022. Small negative floating-point values from convolution are checked and set to zero. The package documentation explains this estimator and its edge correction.

Why planar analysis? The objective is metropolitan screening with an explicitly available polygon window. Chapter 7’s network workflow and the spNetwork documentation highlight a different support: distance along a connected road graph and density per unit road length. A verified historical road graph is not available in this study, so NKDE and network K-functions are not claimed. Planar smoothing can spread intensity across rivers, parallel roads and land between roads. Accordingly, local road-segment priorities require a subsequent network-based assessment with topology, snapping distances, historical coverage and traffic exposure validated. The conditional mark test below preserves the observed accident locations, avoiding uniform redistribution of accidents onto unobserved land for that inference.

Code 
# Retain original naive calendar values; no timezone conversion is made.
month_summary <- points |> st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(month=as.integer(substr(incident_datetime,6,7))) |>
  group_by(month) |> summarise(events=n(),fatal_events=sum(fatal),.groups='drop')
month_summary$days <- c(31,28,31,30,31,30,31,31,30,31,30,31)[month_summary$month]
month_summary$events_per_day <- month_summary$events/month_summary$days
save_plot('monthly', ggplot(month_summary,aes(x=month,y=events_per_day)) +
  geom_col(fill='#217c91',width=.65) + geom_text(aes(label=events),vjust=-.4,size=3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=1:12,labels=month.abb) +
  labs(title='Monthly accident frequency, adjusted for month length',
    subtitle='Bar height: recorded events per calendar day. Labels: event counts.',
    x=NULL,y='Recorded accidents / day',caption='2022 | Six-province window | No traffic-volume adjustment'),height=4.8)
write_csv(month_summary,file.path(out_dir,'monthly.csv'))
# Planar summaries use the actual polygon and projected metre coordinates.
W <- as.owin(st_geometry(study_window))
X <- ppp(xy[,1],xy[,2],window=W,checkdup=FALSE)
stopifnot(npoints(X)==nrow(points))
bws <- c(1000,2000,3000)
kdes <- lapply(bws,function(h) {
  z <- density(X,sigma=h,eps=250,edge=TRUE,at='pixels')
  # FFT convolution can produce tiny negative round-off values far from events.
  stopifnot(min(z$v,na.rm=TRUE) > -1e-10)
  z$v <- pmax(z$v,0); z
})
names(kdes) <- as.character(bws)
kde_data <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(kdes),function(i) {
  dd <- as.data.frame(kdes[[i]]); names(dd) <- c('x','y','density')
  dd$density <- dd$density*1e6
  dd$bandwidth <- paste0(bws[i]/1000,' km'); dd
}))
planar_plot <- ggplot(kde_data,aes(x,y,fill=density)) + geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data=provinces,fill=NA,colour='#7c8795',linewidth=.25,inherit.aes=FALSE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option='magma',trans='sqrt',breaks=c(0,1,5,10,20),
    name='Events / km²',guide=guide_colourbar(barwidth=14)) +
  facet_wrap(~bandwidth,nrow=1) + coord_sf(crs=32647,datum=NA) +
  labs(title='Regional concentration persists across smoothing scales',
    subtitle='Gaussian planar KDE | edge corrected | common colour scale | 250 m grid',x=NULL,y=NULL,
    caption='Bandwidth is Gaussian standard deviation. Land between roads is smoothed; this is not road risk.') +
  theme(axis.text=element_blank(),axis.ticks=element_blank(),legend.position='bottom')
save_plot('planar-kde',planar_plot,12,5.8)
# Bandwidth sensitivity is evaluated on the same non-missing grid cells.
vals <- do.call(cbind,lapply(kdes,function(z)as.vector(z$v)))
vals <- vals[complete.cases(vals),,drop=FALSE]
rank_cor <- cor(vals,method='spearman')
top_overlap <- function(a,b) {
  a <- which(a>=quantile(a,.9)); b <- which(b>=quantile(b,.9))
  length(intersect(a,b))/length(union(a,b))
}
planar_sensitivity <- data.frame(comparison=c('1 vs 2 km','2 vs 3 km'),
  spearman=c(rank_cor[1,2],rank_cor[2,3]),
  top_decile_jaccard=c(top_overlap(vals[,1],vals[,2]),top_overlap(vals[,2],vals[,3])))
write_csv(planar_sensitivity,file.path(out_dir,'planar-sensitivity.csv'))

3.2 Monthly distribution

Interpretation. October has the highest observed daily frequency, 12.71 events per day, compared with 7.57 in February, a ratio of approximately 1.68. October–December contain 1,133 records, or 31.5% of the annual total. Dividing by calendar days removes unequal month length, but does not account for traffic exposure, weather or changes in reporting. These observations support checking late-year workload and exposure data. One annual cycle cannot establish a seasonal mechanism, and the chart does not show that any month is intrinsically more dangerous per journey.

3.3 Planar density and bandwidth sensitivity

Interpretation. High recorded intensity persists around eastern and southern Bangkok and adjoining Samut Prakan, with a northern alignment toward Pathum Thani. At 1 km, separate corridors are visible; at 3 km, nearby alignments merge. The shared colour scale shows that broader smoothing lowers local peaks. Rank correlations exceed 0.90 between adjacent bandwidths, but top-decile overlap is imperfect, so a specific boundary around a hotspot is sensitive to smoothing. These surfaces describe regional concentration, not accident probabilities or density along a road. Their visual detail should not be interpreted as precise junction-level evidence.

All comparisons use the same non-missing grid cells. The top-decile Jaccard statistic is the number of cells shared by the two highest-density deciles divided by the number in either decile. It evaluates map stability, not statistical significance.

3.4 Province-level context

The 159 fatal accidents contain 177 recorded deaths; all retained accidents contain 2,099 recorded injuries. Bangkok has the largest event count, while Pathum Thani has the largest fatal-event count (41). Fatal proportions differ substantially across provinces, which motivates preserving province and reporting-agency totals in the second-order mark test. Province area is a spatial denominator only; it does not control road length, traffic or case ascertainment.

4 Second-order analysis: two different null models

4.1 Uniform-placement benchmark

The first question is whether the complete pattern resembles independent, uniform placement within the study polygon conditional on its observed event count. This conditional complete spatial randomness (CSR) benchmark is intentionally simple. It does not model roads or spatially varying reporting.

The analysis uses Besag’s transformation of Ripley’s K-function,

\[L(r)=\sqrt{K(r)/\pi},\]

and examines \(L(r)-r\) at 250 m steps from 250 m to 5 km. Distances are Euclidean. The border correction uses eligible focal points away from the boundary at each distance, reducing boundary truncation at the cost of losing focal observations. The 5 km upper limit keeps inference at a metropolitan subregional scale. See the L-function documentation.

There are 199 simulations, each containing exactly 3,599 uniformly placed points in the same polygon. With seed 6262022, the global statistic is \(T=\max_r|L(r)-r|\). The Monte Carlo p-value is \((1+\#\{T_b\geq T_{obs}\})/200\). This tests the whole declared distance grid, rather than selecting an attractive pointwise exceedance. The simultaneous band uses the 190th ordered simulated maximum; the p-value resolution is 0.005.

4.2 Fatal-event proximity conditional on accident locations

The more targeted question is whether fatal accidents form more close pairs than expected among recorded accident locations, conditional on both province and reporting agency.

  • Locations and the observation window remain fixed.
  • Fatal/non-fatal labels are permuted within each province × agency group, preserving every group’s number of fatal accidents.
  • The statistic counts unordered fatal–fatal pairs within 250, 500, 1,000 and 2,000 m. Coincident events are retained in the main calculation.
  • 999 permutations use seed 6262023. Pair counts are standardised at each distance using all 1,000 exchangeable configurations, and their maximum forms a one-sided global test for excess proximity. The p-value resolution is 0.001.

The four thresholds span local to corridor-neighbourhood distances while avoiding claims below the uncertain coordinate precision. The test uses Euclidean proximity, not network travel distance or travel time. It is a conditional mark-interaction assessment, not a model of how the road network generates accident locations.

Because every permutation uses exactly the same locations and boundary, the set of potentially observed pairs and its edge truncation remain fixed; no additional point relocation or edge weights are needed for this conditional comparison. The substantive assumption is exchangeability of fatal labels within province–agency groups. Unobserved differences in road type, speed, vehicle mix and reporting can violate it. Groups with no variation in fatal labels contribute no randomisation.

Code 
# Fixed-n homogeneous binomial process in the observed window: conditional CSR.
# This is a diagnostic benchmark, not a test of interaction after controlling roads.
set.seed(6262022)
r_seq <- seq(250,5000,250)
lminus <- function(pattern) {
  z <- Lest(pattern,r=c(0,r_seq),correction='border')
  as.numeric(z$border[-1])-r_seq
}
l_obs <- lminus(X)
nsim_csr <- 199L
l_sims <- replicate(nsim_csr,lminus(runifpoint(npoints(X),win=W)))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(l_obs)),all(is.finite(l_sims)))
t_obs <- max(abs(l_obs)); t_sims <- apply(abs(l_sims),2,max)
csr_p <- (1+sum(t_sims>=t_obs))/(nsim_csr+1)
# Conservative simultaneous 95% envelope, using the 190th of 199 simulated maxima.
critical <- sort(t_sims)[ceiling(.95*(nsim_csr+1))]
csr_table <- data.frame(r_m=r_seq,L_minus_r=l_obs,lower=-critical,upper=critical)
csr_plot <- ggplot(csr_table,aes(r_m/1000,L_minus_r/1000)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=lower/1000,ymax=upper/1000),fill='#b7c9da',alpha=.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0,colour='#64748b',linetype=2) +
  geom_line(colour='#bd4938',linewidth=1) +
  labs(title='The pattern departs strongly from uniform spatial placement',
    subtitle=paste0('Border-corrected L(r) − r | 199 fixed-count simulations | global Monte Carlo p = ',csr_p),
    x='Euclidean distance r (km)',y='L(r) − r (km)',
    caption='Shaded: simultaneous 95% CSR band over 0.25–5 km. Roads and reporting create spatial heterogeneity.')
save_plot('csr-envelope',csr_plot,9,5.5)
write_csv(csr_table,file.path(out_dir,'csr-envelope.csv'))
# Conditional random labelling: preserve positions AND fatal-event totals in every province-agency stratum.
# Unordered pairs; zero-distance pairs are retained in primary analysis.
r_mark <- c(250,500,1000,2000)
pairs <- closepairs(X,rmax=max(r_mark),twice=FALSE,what='ijd')
stopifnot(length(pairs$i)>0)
strata <- interaction(points$spatial_province,points$agency,drop=TRUE)
strata_index <- split(seq_len(nrow(points)),strata)
mark <- as.integer(points$fatal)
pair_counts <- function(m,include_zero=TRUE) {
  dd <- pairs$d[m[pairs$i]==1L & m[pairs$j]==1L & (include_zero | pairs$d>0)]
  vapply(r_mark,function(r)sum(dd<=r),integer(1))
}
nsim_mark <- 999L
set.seed(6262023)
permuted <- replicate(nsim_mark, {
  z <- mark
  for (idx in strata_index) z[idx] <- z[idx][sample.int(length(idx))]
  z
})
mark_obs <- pair_counts(mark)
mark_sims <- apply(permuted,2,pair_counts)
# Symmetric centring/scaling across observed plus simulations preserves exchangeability.
global_mark <- function(observed,simulated) {
  all_counts <- cbind(observed,simulated)
  means <- rowMeans(all_counts); sds <- apply(all_counts,1,sd)
  stopifnot(all(sds>0))
  maxima <- apply(sweep(sweep(all_counts,1,means,'-'),1,sds,'/'),2,max)
  list(p=(1+sum(maxima[-1]>=maxima[1]))/ncol(all_counts),
    statistic=maxima[1],means=means,sds=sds)
}
mark_test <- global_mark(mark_obs,mark_sims)
mark_table <- data.frame(r_m=r_mark,observed_pairs=mark_obs,
  expected_pairs=rowMeans(mark_sims),
  lower=apply(mark_sims,1,quantile,probs=.025),upper=apply(mark_sims,1,quantile,probs=.975))
mark_table$ratio <- mark_table$observed_pairs/mark_table$expected_pairs
save_plot('fatal-pairs',ggplot(mark_table,aes(r_m/1000,observed_pairs)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=lower,ymax=upper),fill='#b7c9da',alpha=.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y=expected_pairs),colour='#217c91',linetype=2,linewidth=.8) +
  geom_line(colour='#bd4938',linewidth=1) + geom_point(colour='#bd4938',size=2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=r_mark/1000) +
  labs(title='Do fatal accidents cluster beyond the observed accident pattern?',
    subtitle=paste0('Province + agency stratified random labels | 999 permutations | one-sided global p = ',mark_test$p),
    x='Euclidean distance threshold (km)',y='Unordered fatal–fatal event pairs',
    caption='Red: observed | Dashed: random-label mean | Shading: pointwise 95% intervals (not a global envelope).'),9,5.6)
write_csv(mark_table,file.path(out_dir,'fatal-pairs.csv'))

4.3 Results: all accidents against CSR

Interpretation. The observed pattern departs from conditional CSR (global p = 0.005); the largest absolute deviation in \(L(r)-r\) is approximately 5.01 km over the tested grid. The positive curve is consistent with the corridor concentrations visible in the maps. However, the null places points uniformly on the entire polygon, including land without represented roads. Its rejection demonstrates spatial non-uniformity, not crash contagion or interaction independent of first-order intensity. The result therefore motivates the conditional fatal-label comparison rather than proving that nearby accidents cause one another.

4.4 Results: fatal accidents against conditional random labels

Interpretation. At 1 km there are 52 fatal–fatal pairs, compared with a permutation mean of 90.6. All four observed counts are below their random-label means. The one-sided global p-value is 0.998, giving no evidence of excess fatal-event proximity after conditioning on province, agency and accident locations. This does not confirm random labelling, prove spatial inhibition or show that dense corridors are safe. Shaded intervals are pointwise descriptions; the stated global test is the inferential result. Different fatality processes or reporting patterns may explain the lower counts.

5 Robustness and integrated findings

Code 
# Same random permutations, but omit all coincident pairs.
nozero_obs <- pair_counts(mark,FALSE)
nozero_sims <- apply(permuted,2,pair_counts,include_zero=FALSE)
nozero_test <- global_mark(nozero_obs,nozero_sims)
# Unstratified random labels are a deliberately less-adjusted comparison.
set.seed(6262024)
unstrat_sims <- replicate(nsim_mark,pair_counts(sample(mark)))
unstrat_test <- global_mark(mark_obs,unstrat_sims)
# CSR diagnostic after reducing repeated coordinates to one location each.
Xu <- X[!duplicated(loc_key)]
set.seed(6262025)
lu_obs <- lminus(Xu)
lu_sims <- replicate(nsim_csr,lminus(runifpoint(npoints(Xu),win=W)))
unique_csr_p <- (1+sum(apply(abs(lu_sims),2,max)>=max(abs(lu_obs))))/(nsim_csr+1)
stats_summary <- list(csr_p=csr_p,csr_max_deviation_m=t_obs,csr_unique_p=unique_csr_p,
  fatal_pair_p=mark_test$p,fatal_pair_nozero_p=nozero_test$p,
  fatal_pair_unstratified_p=unstrat_test$p,n_close_pairs=length(pairs$i),
  n_zero_pairs=sum(pairs$d==0),month_peak=month.abb[month_summary$month[which.max(month_summary$events_per_day)]],
  month_low=month.abb[month_summary$month[which.min(month_summary$events_per_day)]])
jsonlite::write_json(list(quality=quality,statistics=stats_summary),file.path(out_dir,'summary.json'),pretty=TRUE,auto_unbox=TRUE)
print(stats_summary); print(mark_table); print(planar_sensitivity)

Repeated coordinates do not explain the broad departure from uniformity. Reducing the pattern from 3,599 accidents to 3,278 unique recorded locations still gives a CSR p-value of 0.005. This sensitivity changes the unit to a recorded location, so it is not the primary event-level result.

The absence of excess fatal-event proximity is stable under the checks used. Removing all zero-distance pairs gives p = 0.998; removing the province–agency stratification gives p = 0.995. The latter comparison is deliberately less adjusted and does not replace the primary conditional model. Both tests remain one-sided for clustering, so a large p-value is not evidence for uniformity or absence of all spatial structure.

First- and second-order results answer different questions. The KDE locates high recorded accident intensity, and the CSR result confirms the pattern’s non-uniformity against a simple benchmark. The fatal-label result addresses whether severe outcomes are especially concentrated relative to those already observed locations. It supplies no evidence of extra clustering at the declared scales. High-volume corridors and fatal-event locations therefore deserve complementary scrutiny, rather than being treated as interchangeable maps.

The bandwidth comparisons retain a stable broad concentration while shifting the boundaries of high-density zones. None of the sensitivity checks removes the core limitations: incomplete agency coverage, selective missing coordinates, uncertain positional accuracy, absent exposure and the use of planar distances. The tests are exploratory assessments of this dataset and window, not causal or predictive models.

6 Public-safety planning and management

Use the density maps as an initial screen for coordinated corridor reviews in Bangkok and adjoining provinces. The persistence of broad concentrations across 1–3 km bandwidths supports regional prioritisation, while their changing fine detail argues for inspecting original records and road geometry before naming a junction or road segment for intervention.

Maintain a separate review of fatal accidents. Pathum Thani and Samut Prakan contain more fatal events than Bangkok in the retained sample, despite lower total event counts. The conditional test does not support extra fatal-event clustering at the investigated distances. Consequently, a programme focused solely on the highest-density zones could overlook dispersed severe outcomes. Review fatal cases individually alongside corridor-level workload.

Repair the reporting gap before comparing expressway performance. The 189 ungeolocated records all belong to Bangkok’s expressway reporting agency. Recovering their original location references and matching them to verified road geometry would improve both coverage and the fairness of geographic comparisons. Repeated coordinates also warrant checking against route and kilometre-post information.

The higher recorded daily frequency in October–December provides a reason to review late-year response workload, traffic volumes and operating conditions. It does not establish a recurring seasonal hazard. Validate the pattern against additional years and reporting changes before committing seasonal resources.

Before selecting physical measures, obtain a connected road network appropriate to 2022, traffic exposure, road geometry, speed observations and road-user composition. Network density and severity-specific rates could then support more precise site screening. Validate candidate sites through engineering inspection and local evidence. These data alone cannot justify a causal claim about speeding, prescribe a particular design intervention, or establish its expected safety benefit. Evaluate implemented measures with suitable comparison locations and allowance for changes in exposure and regression to the mean.

7 Reproducibility and analytical checks

Every analytical operation and figure is produced with R. This report executes labelled sections from R/prepare.R and R/analysis.R; opening a code block shows the code used. The same saved figures are reused in the presentation. No external analytical outputs are pasted into the workflow.

The scripts check input parsing, event-ID uniqueness, finite coordinates, valid geometries, complete casualty counts, the point-pattern size and finite simulation results. Original inputs are checked by SHA-256. Seeds 6262022–6262025 are fixed and independent across the simulation comparisons. The report, source scripts and generated site are kept together in the repository. See the reproduction guide for a clean RStudio run and acquisition instructions.

::: {.callout-note title="Study in brief"}
The analysis covers **3,599 geolocated accident records**, including **159 fatal accidents**, within Bangkok and five neighbouring provinces in 2022. Recorded accidents concentrate along metropolitan corridors. Their spatial pattern differs strongly from uniform placement, but fatal accidents do **not** show excess close-pair clustering relative to the observed accident locations after accounting for province and reporting agency. These findings support corridor screening and improvements to reporting coverage; they do not estimate the probability of a crash per journey.
:::

## Research question and scope

**Where do recorded accidents concentrate in Greater Bangkok, how does their frequency vary during 2022, and are fatal accidents unusually close to one another after accounting for the geography of reported accidents?**

The intended audience is metropolitan transport planners and road-safety teams. Three distinctions guide the study:

1. **Intensity:** the number of recorded events per unit area or calendar day.
2. **Second-order structure:** how event pairs are distributed over distance, relative to a stated random model.
3. **Risk:** the probability of an accident for a given amount of travel. Traffic volumes, vehicle-kilometres and consistent reporting denominators are unavailable, so risk is not estimated.

The unit of analysis is an **accident record identified by `acc_code`**, rather than a casualty or vehicle. A fatal accident has `number_of_fatalities > 0`; one such accident can contain several deaths. All accident types are included. Presumed causes are not treated as established causal explanations.

### Sources, coverage and provenance

| [geoBoundaries gbOpen THA ADM1](https://www.geoboundaries.org/api/current/gbOpen/THA/ADM1/) | 77 administrative areas; metadata vintage **2017**; boundary ID `THA-ADM1-36821470`; accessed 27 September 2026 | Study boundary; **ODbL 1.0**, upstream OpenStreetMap contributors and Wambacher |

The original CSV contains 18 columns covering identifiers, dates, province, reporting agency, accident attributes, casualties and coordinates. The source has no traffic exposure or coordinate-accuracy measure. Its records come from three road agencies, so it cannot be assumed to enumerate every accident on every local street.

The [download manifest](data/metadata/downloads.json), [Kaggle metadata](data/metadata/kaggle.json) and [boundary metadata](data/metadata/geoboundaries-adm1.json) preserve acquisition dates, versions and SHA-256 checksums. The boundary downloader uses a fixed repository revision. Raw files remain separate from analytical outputs.

### Study extent, dates and coordinates

The study area comprises **Bangkok, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Samut Prakan, Samut Sakhon and Nakhon Pathom**. These are selected by administrative ISO codes `TH-10`, `TH-12`, `TH-13`, `TH-11`, `TH-74` and `TH-73`. Their dissolved union forms the observation window; it is not the rectangular map extent. Province labels in the CSV serve as a quality check, while polygon intersection determines spatial inclusion.

The analysis uses **incident dates from 1 January to 31 December 2022**, inclusive. Dates are read as written, without converting an unspecified source timezone. The reporting date is not substituted for the incident date. Monthly counts are divided by each month's number of calendar days; a single year supports description, not a claim of recurring seasonality.

Longitude and latitude are interpreted as WGS 84 because they are supplied as geographic coordinates. This source-CRS assumption is a limitation. They are transformed to **WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647)**, appropriate for the region's longitude and metre-based analysis. Province geometries are validated before union. The older boundary vintage is disclosed; this study does not establish that every local boundary was unchanged between 2017 and 2022.

## First-order analysis: intensity across space and time

### Methods and parameter choices

Monthly events per day provide a transparent temporal description. Spatial intensity is estimated with a **Gaussian planar kernel density estimator (KDE)**, using each event with weight one. The primary smoothing scale is **2 km**, with **1 km and 3 km** alternatives. These are declared regional screening scales, not a statistically optimal junction-level bandwidth. A common **250 m grid** provides four cells per smallest bandwidth and eight per primary bandwidth.

The `spatstat.explore::density.ppp()` edge correction compensates for kernel mass outside the observation window. Densities calculated per square metre are multiplied by one million to give **recorded events per km² for 2022**. Small negative floating-point values from convolution are checked and set to zero. The [package documentation](https://rdrr.io/cran/spatstat.explore/man/density.ppp.html) explains this estimator and its edge correction.

**Why planar analysis?** The objective is metropolitan screening with an explicitly available polygon window. Chapter 7's [network workflow](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap07) and the [spNetwork documentation](https://jeremygelb.github.io/spNetwork/reference/index.html) highlight a different support: distance along a connected road graph and density per unit road length. A verified historical road graph is not available in this study, so NKDE and network K-functions are not claimed. Planar smoothing can spread intensity across rivers, parallel roads and land between roads. Accordingly, local road-segment priorities require a subsequent network-based assessment with topology, snapping distances, historical coverage and traffic exposure validated. The conditional mark test below preserves the observed accident locations, avoiding uniform redistribution of accidents onto unobserved land for that inference.

![Recorded accidents per calendar day by month, with monthly event totals above each bar.](figures/monthly.png){#fig-monthly fig-alt="Monthly accident counts divided by days in the month; October has the highest daily frequency and February the lowest."}

::: {.visual-interpretation}
**Interpretation.** October has the highest observed daily frequency, **12.71 events per day**, compared with **7.57 in February**, a ratio of approximately **1.68**. October–December contain **1,133 records**, or **31.5%** of the annual total. Dividing by calendar days removes unequal month length, but does not account for traffic exposure, weather or changes in reporting. These observations support checking late-year workload and exposure data. One annual cycle cannot establish a seasonal mechanism, and the chart does not show that any month is intrinsically more dangerous per journey.
:::

### Planar density and bandwidth sensitivity

![Edge-corrected planar KDE at 1, 2 and 3 km Gaussian bandwidths, on the same grid and colour scale.](figures/planar-kde.png){#fig-kde fig-alt="Three density maps with identical colour scale; narrow corridor detail at one kilometre merges into broader concentrations at two and three kilometres."}

::: {.visual-interpretation}
**Interpretation.** High recorded intensity persists around eastern and southern Bangkok and adjoining Samut Prakan, with a northern alignment toward Pathum Thani. At 1 km, separate corridors are visible; at 3 km, nearby alignments merge. The shared colour scale shows that broader smoothing lowers local peaks. Rank correlations exceed 0.90 between adjacent bandwidths, but top-decile overlap is imperfect, so a specific boundary around a hotspot is sensitive to smoothing. These surfaces describe regional concentration, not accident probabilities or density along a road. Their visual detail should not be interpreted as precise junction-level evidence.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bandwidth
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(planar_sensitivity,digits=3,
  col.names=c("Bandwidth comparison","Spearman rank correlation","Top-decile Jaccard overlap"),
  caption="Stability of planar density surfaces across smoothing scales.")
```

All comparisons use the same non-missing grid cells. The top-decile Jaccard statistic is the number of cells shared by the two highest-density deciles divided by the number in either decile. It evaluates map stability, not statistical significance.

## Second-order analysis: two different null models

### Uniform-placement benchmark

The first question is whether the complete pattern resembles **independent, uniform placement within the study polygon conditional on its observed event count**. This conditional complete spatial randomness (CSR) benchmark is intentionally simple. It does not model roads or spatially varying reporting.

The analysis uses Besag's transformation of Ripley's K-function,

$$L(r)=\sqrt{K(r)/\pi},$$

and examines $L(r)-r$ at **250 m steps from 250 m to 5 km**. Distances are Euclidean. The **border correction** uses eligible focal points away from the boundary at each distance, reducing boundary truncation at the cost of losing focal observations. The 5 km upper limit keeps inference at a metropolitan subregional scale. See the [L-function documentation](https://rdrr.io/cran/spatstat.explore/man/Lest.html).

There are **199 simulations**, each containing exactly `r fmt(quality$n)` uniformly placed points in the same polygon. With seed **6262022**, the global statistic is $T=\max_r|L(r)-r|$. The Monte Carlo p-value is $(1+\#\{T_b\geq T_{obs}\})/200$. This tests the whole declared distance grid, rather than selecting an attractive pointwise exceedance. The simultaneous band uses the 190th ordered simulated maximum; the p-value resolution is 0.005.

### Fatal-event proximity conditional on accident locations

The more targeted question is whether **fatal accidents form more close pairs than expected among recorded accident locations**, conditional on both province and reporting agency.

- Locations and the observation window remain fixed.
- Fatal/non-fatal labels are permuted **within each province × agency group**, preserving every group's number of fatal accidents.
- The statistic counts **unordered fatal–fatal pairs** within **250, 500, 1,000 and 2,000 m**. Coincident events are retained in the main calculation.
- **999 permutations** use seed **6262023**. Pair counts are standardised at each distance using all 1,000 exchangeable configurations, and their maximum forms a **one-sided global test for excess proximity**. The p-value resolution is 0.001.

The four thresholds span local to corridor-neighbourhood distances while avoiding claims below the uncertain coordinate precision. The test uses Euclidean proximity, not network travel distance or travel time. It is a conditional mark-interaction assessment, not a model of how the road network generates accident locations.

Because every permutation uses exactly the same locations and boundary, the set of potentially observed pairs and its edge truncation remain fixed; no additional point relocation or edge weights are needed for this conditional comparison. The substantive assumption is exchangeability of fatal labels within province–agency groups. Unobserved differences in road type, speed, vehicle mix and reporting can violate it. Groups with no variation in fatal labels contribute no randomisation.

::: {.visual-interpretation}
**Interpretation.** The observed pattern departs from conditional CSR (**global p = `r format.pval(csr_p,digits=3,eps=.001)`**); the largest absolute deviation in $L(r)-r$ is approximately **`r round(t_obs/1000,2)` km** over the tested grid. The positive curve is consistent with the corridor concentrations visible in the maps. However, the null places points uniformly on the entire polygon, including land without represented roads. Its rejection demonstrates spatial non-uniformity, not crash contagion or interaction independent of first-order intensity. The result therefore motivates the conditional fatal-label comparison rather than proving that nearby accidents cause one another.
:::

All four observed counts are below their random-label means. The one-sided global p-value is **`r mark_test$p`**, giving no evidence of **excess** fatal-event proximity after conditioning on province, agency and accident locations. This does not confirm random labelling, prove spatial inhibition or show that dense corridors are safe. Shaded intervals are pointwise descriptions; the stated global test is the inferential result. Different fatality processes or reporting patterns may explain the lower counts.

```{r}
knitr::kable(mark_table,digits=2,col.names=c("Distance (m)","Observed pairs","Permutation mean",
  "Pointwise 2.5%","Pointwise 97.5%","Observed / expected"),
  caption="Fatal-event pairs against the province-and-agency conditional null.")
```

## Robustness and integrated findings

```{r}
#| label: thx-sensitivity
#| results: hide
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-robustness
#| echo: false
robustness <- data.frame(Analysis=c("CSR: all accident records","CSR: one point per recorded location",
  "Fatal labels: province + agency strata","Fatal labels: strata, excluding coincident pairs",
  "Fatal labels: no strata"),
  `Global p`=c(csr_p,unique_csr_p,mark_test$p,nozero_test$p,unstrat_test$p),check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(robustness,digits=3,caption="Global tests under alternative treatments of repeated locations and labels.")
```

**Repeated coordinates do not explain the broad departure from uniformity.** Reducing the pattern from `r fmt(quality$n)` accidents to `r fmt(quality$unique_locations)` unique recorded locations still gives a CSR p-value of `r unique_csr_p`. This sensitivity changes the unit to a recorded location, so it is not the primary event-level result.

**The absence of excess fatal-event proximity is stable under the checks used.** Removing all zero-distance pairs gives p = `r nozero_test$p`; removing the province–agency stratification gives p = `r unstrat_test$p`. The latter comparison is deliberately less adjusted and does not replace the primary conditional model. Both tests remain one-sided for clustering, so a large p-value is not evidence for uniformity or absence of all spatial structure.

**First- and second-order results answer different questions.** The KDE locates high recorded accident intensity, and the CSR result confirms the pattern's non-uniformity against a simple benchmark. The fatal-label result addresses whether severe outcomes are especially concentrated relative to those already observed locations. It supplies no evidence of extra clustering at the declared scales. High-volume corridors and fatal-event locations therefore deserve complementary scrutiny, rather than being treated as interchangeable maps.

The bandwidth comparisons retain a stable broad concentration while shifting the boundaries of high-density zones. None of the sensitivity checks removes the core limitations: incomplete agency coverage, selective missing coordinates, uncertain positional accuracy, absent exposure and the use of planar distances. The tests are exploratory assessments of this dataset and window, not causal or predictive models.

## Public-safety planning and management

::: {.planning-discussion}
Use the density maps as an initial screen for coordinated corridor reviews in Bangkok and adjoining provinces. The persistence of broad concentrations across 1–3 km bandwidths supports regional prioritisation, while their changing fine detail argues for inspecting original records and road geometry before naming a junction or road segment for intervention.

Maintain a separate review of fatal accidents. Pathum Thani and Samut Prakan contain more fatal events than Bangkok in the retained sample, despite lower total event counts. The conditional test does not support extra fatal-event clustering at the investigated distances. Consequently, a programme focused solely on the highest-density zones could overlook dispersed severe outcomes. Review fatal cases individually alongside corridor-level workload.

Repair the reporting gap before comparing expressway performance. The 189 ungeolocated records all belong to Bangkok's expressway reporting agency. Recovering their original location references and matching them to verified road geometry would improve both coverage and the fairness of geographic comparisons. Repeated coordinates also warrant checking against route and kilometre-post information.

The higher recorded daily frequency in October–December provides a reason to review late-year response workload, traffic volumes and operating conditions. It does not establish a recurring seasonal hazard. Validate the pattern against additional years and reporting changes before committing seasonal resources.

Before selecting physical measures, obtain a connected road network appropriate to 2022, traffic exposure, road geometry, speed observations and road-user composition. Network density and severity-specific rates could then support more precise site screening. Validate candidate sites through engineering inspection and local evidence. These data alone cannot justify a causal claim about speeding, prescribe a particular design intervention, or establish its expected safety benefit. Evaluate implemented measures with suitable comparison locations and allowance for changes in exposure and regression to the mean.
:::

## Reproducibility and analytical checks

Every analytical operation and figure is produced with R. This report executes labelled sections from [`R/prepare.R`](R/prepare.R) and [`R/analysis.R`](R/analysis.R); opening a code block shows the code used. The same saved figures are reused in the presentation. No external analytical outputs are pasted into the workflow.

The scripts check input parsing, event-ID uniqueness, finite coordinates, valid geometries, complete casualty counts, the point-pattern size and finite simulation results. Original inputs are checked by SHA-256. Seeds **6262022–6262025** are fixed and independent across the simulation comparisons. The report, source scripts and generated site are kept together in the repository. See the [reproduction guide](learning-guide.qmd) for a clean RStudio run and acquisition instructions.
